canonicalExplanation.summary: Four different things share the word "Java". The **Java language** is the rules for writing `.java` source. The **JDK** (Java Development Kit) is the toolbox: `javac` (the compiler), `java` (the launcher), `jshell`, `jar` and more. **Bytecode** is what `javac` produces: `.class` files full of portable instructions, not machine code. The **JVM** (Java Virtual Machine) **loads**, **verifies** and **runs** bytecode, compiling hot code to machine code as it goes (JIT) and managing memory with a garbage collector. They're versioned too: bytecode compiled for Java 21 won't run on an older JVM, which reports an `UnsupportedClassVersionError`.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A learner hears "Java" used for the language, the download, the `java` command and the thing that crashed with a version error, and assumes they're all one program. Their Main.class, built on Java 21, won't run on a server that has Java 17. The learner traces Main.java through javac into Main.class and then explains why java launches a JVM rather than interpreting the source file as ordinary text. In this lesson you'll trace a Java source file through compilation and JVM execution.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know **Source-to-execution models** (programs run on a machine) and **Editor and terminal workflow** (running commands).

sections.heading: The model: source, bytecode, virtual machine
sections.body:
```java
// Main.java
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Hello from the JVM");
    }
}
```

```bash
javac Main.java        # JDK compiler: checks the language rules, writes Main.class.
ls                     # Main.java  Main.class
javap -c Main          # peek at the bytecode instructions (optional).
java Main              # starts a JVM, loads Main.class, runs main.
java -version          # which JVM will run it?
```

| Piece | What it is |
|---|---|
| Java language. | the syntax and rules in .java files. |
| JDK. | tools: javac, java, jshell, jar. |
| bytecode (.class). | portable compiled instructions. |
| JVM. | loads, verifies, JIT-compiles and runs bytecode. |

```reveal
{"prompt": "Doesn't `java Main.java` run source directly?", "answer": "Since Java 11, the launcher can take a single source file: it compiles it in memory with the compiler first, then runs the bytecode on the JVM. The JVM still only executes bytecode."}
```

examples.title: From Main.java to a running JVM
examples.situation: The learner traces Main.java through javac into Main.class and then explains why java launches a JVM rather than interpreting the source file as ordinary text.
walkthrough: **The learner traces Main.java through javac into Main.class:** javac checks the source and writes bytecode.
**Then explains why java launches a JVM:** java Main starts a virtual machine that loads and verifies Main.class.
**Rather than interpreting the source file as ordinary text:** the JVM will run bytecode, JIT-compiling hot code to machine code.
examples.result: The learner can name every stage, and the version error makes sense.

examples.title: The server version error
examples.situation: A build compiled with JDK 21 fails on a Java 17 server with UnsupportedClassVersionError.
walkthrough: Either upgrade the server's JVM to 21,
or compile with javac --release 17 (and avoid newer APIs).
examples.result: The same bytecode runs on the intended server.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: The JDK, Java language, bytecode, and JVM are four names for the same component and always have the same version behavior.
misconceptions.correction: They're separate: the language defines source rules, the JDK provides tools, bytecode is the compiled format, and the JVM executes it. Each has versions that must be compatible.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In "The server version error", which two pieces disagreed?

analogy.example: Java is like **publishing a recipe in a universal notation**. The language is how you write the recipe; javac is **the translator** into the notation (bytecode); the JVM is **a robot kitchen** that reads the notation on any machine. An older robot can't read a newer notation edition.
limitations: Robots don't learn on the job; the JVM's JIT does speed up hot code.
The JDK is the whole writer's toolkit.

recap.summary: To trace a Java program, remember javac from the JDK checks the language rules and compiles .java source into .class bytecode, and the java launcher starts a JVM that loads, verifies and executes that bytecode, with versions that must be compatible between compiler target and JVM.
